exact_prompt:
I'm shopping for cottage cheese in the United States.

I've never tried cottage cheese. Which brand would you recommend for a first purchase, and why?
reviewed_answer:
Welcome to the wonderful, slightly polarizing world of cottage cheese! Because it’s your first time, your introduction matters a lot—some cheaper or overly watery brands can turn people off instantly with a chalky texture or a sour, chemical-like bite.   

Two standout brands dominate American grocery shelves as the absolute best choices for a first-timer, depending on what you're looking for:

Top Recommendation: Good Culture (Classic 2% or Whole Milk 4%)

If you want the brand that has won over millions of former cottage cheese skeptics, look for Good Culture (usually found in a distinct cup with a bright blue or orange label).

Why it’s great for beginners: It has an exceptionally thick, creamy, and velvety texture rather than swimming in a watery liquid. It also features live and active probiotics, which give it a clean, mild, pleasantly tangy flavor profile (reminiscent of high-end sour cream or Greek yogurt) without any weird chemical or bitter aftertastes.   

The ingredient list: It's remarkably clean—mostly just organic skim milk, cream, sea salt, and live cultures. No gums, thickeners, or strange additives.   

The Classic Alternative: Daisy (Whole Milk 4%)

If you can’t find Good Culture, Daisy is the quintessential, widely available gold standard.   

Why it’s great for beginners: Daisy is famous for keeping things traditional. Their 4% whole milk cottage cheese uses just milk, cream, and salt (no gums or stabilizers). The curds are tender, the surrounding cream is rich, and it has a very reliable, quintessential dairy taste that isn't overly aggressive.   

Quick Tips for Your First Taste

Choose Your Curd Size: Cottage cheese comes in small curd or large curd. Small curd is more uniform and easier to start with if texture is a concern.   

Fat Percentage Matters: If you want the richest, most comforting flavor, go for 4% milkfat (whole milk). If you prefer something lighter with a bit more tang, try 2% milkfat.

How to Eat It:

Savory: Try a scoop with a heavy crack of fresh black pepper, a drizzle of good olive oil, and some sliced cherry tomatoes or cucumbers.

Sweet: Go the classic route by topping it with fresh fruit (like pineapple chunks, peaches, or berries) and a drizzle of honey.   

Are you leaning toward trying it sweet with fruit, or keeping it savory with salt and pepper?
